newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rescuers face danger in search for bodies.
newsitem.headline: Peru rescuers face danger in search for bodies.

text.p: Peruvian rescue workers were praying for fine weather on Friday as they prepared to resume the dangerous task of digging for the corpses of up to 300 peasants buried in Tuesday's massive Andean mudslide.

Working in the wet under dense clouds, rescuers used picks, spades and their bare hands until rain helped unleash a fresh mudslide, which forced them to call a halt for the day around lunchtime on Thursday.

A column of soldiers carried jugs of gasoline and fumigators to burn and disinfect decomposing bodies of horses, cows and pigs, while distraught families sought desperately to identify the 43 mangled human corpses dug up so far.
Hundreds of survivors from the two mountainside villages that were destroyed passed their second night in makeshift shelters and government shelters.

They told harrowing stories of the torrent of mud and rocks that crashed down on them before dawn on Tuesday. Peru's mountain-dwellers have always feared the rainy season's sudden mudslides, which they know by the Quechua Indian word "Huayco."

Jose Saavedra, 40, ran out of the path of the mudslide just before seeing his home engulfed. "It was all so quick," he said. "I just saw my house collapse with my family and I could not do anything ... The entire population has disappeared."
But many corpses were likely to remain entombed forever as the 30-foot (10 metre)-deep mud was expected to harden before they could be located.
"It is most likely that many bodies are not going to be retrieved," Civil Defence official and local Mayor Luis Barra Pacheco told Reuters.
The Civil Defence said it was flying in eight sniffer dogs to help locate bodies closest to the mud's surface.

Tuesday's mudslide buried the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra in a remote mountainous region of southeast Peru. A smaller landslide on Thursday morning covered the few remaining roofs of houses in Ccocha that had been poking out of the mud.
Civil Defence officials feared the rain might send more mud slamming into scores of workers at the base of the slide.
The authorities tried to persuade hundreds of people from three nearby communities to move, but the people of Kerapata, closest to the disaster site, refused to leave their animals.

In the nearby village of Tamburco, relatives of the dead waited in lines in the rain to enter a makeshift morgue in a schoolhouse. Inside, mourners dressed in black arranged the clothing of their dead loved ones who were awaiting burial in black, gray and yellow coffins.

Dina Rivas Tapia stared up the hill from Kerapata's town square to the landslide, handkerchief in hand. "My entire family has disappeared. They were 25 people. I have no house, no money, I don't even have a bed."

A mass was said later on Thursday for the victims by the Bishop of Abancay, Isidro Sala Rivera. "Pain is a mystery," he told hundreds of grieving worshippers on the steps of the church in Tamburco, "but it is a mystery scored by faith."

Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer warned of possible epidemics among the 250 to 600 families left homeless. The Japanese Embassy in Lima announced it was donating $220,000 in cash, tents and blankets for those left homeless.

President Alberto Fujimori, who visited where Ccocha and Pumaranra had been, on Thursday moved on to another disaster zone in the northern region of San Martin. Amazon floodwaters from heavy rains there triggered a mudslide that destroyed the homes of 500 families.
A woman and two children were swept away in Yuracyacu, and another 100 people were reported missing in the isolated area.

After surveying the floods by helicopter, Fujimori promised aid for the stricken. "Despite these difficulties, I see you determined to carry on," he said. "On top of that will and decision, the government wants to help with small contributions to lay the foundations."
